items.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024
items.q: But they’ve all got the same skills and they all applied them in their own way. Not my way, their way. ... take Ari Hoenig and Keith Carlock — ooh, night and day.

ctx.x: Let me ask you, go back to your teaching for a minute. If you can think back to the start of your career, the early years, an advice that you might have given a senior — or a junior or a senior drummer who, you know like a music major, how might it be different from the advice you would give near the end of your teaching career?

Oh jeez. I can’t answer that. I don’t know. I’ll tell you why I can’t answer it. It’s because everybody’s different. And my philosophy became, when I first started out and how I related to a student is I was dead set on making this person the greatest drummer in the world, and which I realized later on was just a huge ego trip on my part, so that I could say I created that drummer. And I realized that not everybody is meant to be the greatest drummer in the world — whatever that means — but I realized that my job…

my teaching is none of my students play like me. I mean that’s the greatest compliment ever that a teacher can be given. And they’re all distinct personalities. Everybody — take Ari Hoenig and Keith Carlock — ooh, night and day. You know? Rich Redman, the country drummer? Night and day. But they’ve all got the same skills and they all applied them in their own way. Not my way, their way. It’s just like you teach somebody language. They learn how to use it their way. That’s the same thing you do with music, with…
